pr_title: Skip constructor when entity is loaded from database
pr_comments: Looks like a big hack. What if user **wants** to have something initialized in the constructor?
Im going to close it, thanks for your efforts.

@pleerock I agree. It is big hack, but correct behavior in my opinion. I was inspired by Doctrine ORM. When entity is deserialized from db, constructor is omitted by reflection. So you have free constructor for initial checks and you don't need write special hack for undefined values.

To answer your question: If someone want to initialize something during deserialization from db, there is event (http://typeorm.io/#/listeners-and-subscribers/afterload)

@pleerock 

I agree that calling constructor during deserialization is a wrong behavior and suggest to merge this.

1. You noticed that constructor can have additional logic, but in the most cases this logic is invalid during deserialization process. Very simple example is assigning properties in constructor. As user doesn't expect undefined here it will cause crashing in runtime. Here are multiple bugs reported related to this.
2. It is near impossible to use typeorm in 'strict' compiler mode. Especially, if you want to get some additional safety.
3. Direct assignments of prototypes is more-less well known approach in js world.
Reopening this issue and according PR.
I think I have change my mind since I see people have inconvenience with strict mode. @Kononnable @vlapo @havenchyk what you think about it?
@pleerock Wow, glad to hear it! Tell me if you need some help

There are reasons why some libraries requires such classes(e.g. entity classes) to have a constructor without parameters. 

I'm good with both solutions:
- not calling a constructor(since it's deserialization) as long as there is a way to easy propagate fields not saved in db(without a Column decorator)
- use default values and constructor without parameters(current implementation)
We can achieve same results with both of them so it's just a matter of preference.
Will this PR make strict mode usable?
I can merge this branch if it fix all issues and will be created against `next`

So I tried to do just that. I basically copied the code (submitted by @pepakriz into a new branch created against `next`, only I used JS `Reflect` instead of `ObjectInstantiator`).

https://github.com/XanderEmu/typeorm/tree/skip-constructor-when-entity-is-loaded-from-the-database

The tests are failing for `entity-metadata-validator > initialized relations` which `should throw error if relation with initialized array was found on many-to-many relation`.

I'm not sure how should I proceed. Basically, I don't understand why this is the case. Perhaps, with the change proposed by @pepakriz, it is not a problem anymore?

@XanderEmu I'll need to check tests on `next`, maybe they are failing not because of your changes. Just create a PR with all changes you propose, make sure your test is passing and I'll take of the rest once I get a chance to review and merge it.

I'm afraid they weren't failing on next. I submitted a PR anyway:
https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/pull/3845

I am good with both solution too. But I have to say that most of my entity classes have a lot of properties so mostly I use only one parameter with data to initialize and always optional. 

Right now we have some issues and questions about parameters in constructor, after merge we will have question/issues about "non called constructors". So if this change will merged we have to update documentation and inform developers about deserialization process.

@vlapo If you are using strict mode, Typescript complains if you have a non optional property on a class that is not explicitly instantiated in the constructor. This seems like a pretty integral part of type correctness to me.

If you are using an optional argument to instantiate your entities, are you doing a null check every time you access a property on an entity? If not, it seems like you are missing out on some of the correctness checking that Typescript could provide.

@pepakriz nice work. I was about to submit a PR tackling the same issue, and I stumbled upon your work.

The example you have implemented in your test cases underline the right behavior the ORM should have in my opinion. With this solution, and with a Domain-Driven-Design standpoint: the business process of creating domain object and the technical process of re-creation/hydratation of these pre-existing domain objects are clearly separated.

NHibernate for example requires to have a default constructor on the domain classes (that you would usually hide by marking it as `protected`) to tackle the same design principle of separating an initial object creation (by the user) from its re-creation by the ORM later on.

Here the solution provided is even more elegant, as it does not require polluting domain classes with useless empty constructor (useless as they add no business meaning to your domain).

PS: just for information, I was using `return Reflect.construct(function() {}, [], this.target);` in my intended PR, end-result is same apparently I guess.
Closing in favor of #3845 . @pepakriz thanks for the contribution!

issue_context.title: Skip constructor when entity is loaded from database
comments: @lodemo I've already tried your solution, but It leads to error: `error TS2564: Property 'title' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor.`

Correct, you should understand what each compile option will bring it, value of it and how you are going to use it. You either need to use @lodemo solution either initialize your property in the constructor.

I'll close this issue since its not related to TypeORM and more related to language itself. Feel free to keep discussion.

Thanks for your answers. I like strict typing and I would like use it with this library. I want correct signatures in constructors - `title?: string` vs `title: string`. So this is reason for my proposal about skipping constructor call. My PR https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/pull/1773 contains big hack in entity deserialization, but I don't have to write next hacks in entity constructors. Look at Doctrine ORM project. They do the same thing and they have lifecycle event `postLoad` (http://docs.doctrine-project.org/projects/doctrine-orm/en/latest/reference/events.html#lifecycle-events)

Edit: yeah, typeorm has similar event - http://typeorm.io/#/listeners-and-subscribers/afterload

Sorry, but I think avoiding a constructor and having users to use a listener instead is a bad idea. If you want to keep strictness you should initialize your properties, e.g. `title: string = "";` - that's a proper resolution of the problem.

Why bad idea? In my opinion, deserialization is not the same as creating a new instance. I suggest skipping constructor only when an entity is deserialized from db, because the constructor is called without arguments and correct arguments cannot be estimated. The constructor should validate own consistency, so nobody can create an object in an invalid state. `afterLoad` event was the answer to the question: `What if user wants to have something initialized after load?`. But anyway, I've never used it.

In canonical DDD, you just cannot have an aggregate root entity constructor without a required argument (there's ID at least). Of course, there's an obvious workaround: using a named constructor (implemented with a static method) and declaring the constructor private kind of solves the issue. But a good ORM should not put such restrictions on model design.

In Javascript, there is a proper way of creating a new instance without invoking constructor, no hacks required:

```
Object.create(objectClass.prototype);
```
Reopening this issue and according PR.

Yes I found that after I posted it and forgot to update this example. I apologize but I was just trying to be helpful. And I do believe that the rough idea is still gets be going where the want to go.

Definitely agree with this issue, you shouldn't have to change your constructor for the sake of your ORM. Could someone tell me why TypeORM calls the constructor in the first place? Seems like an odd design choice to me, since it won't have the required arguments.

This calls the constructor becuase that is how you create an object.  Such as the entity.  

Anyone have suggestions on how we can instantiate the object without calling the constructor?  Won't this break the paradigms and promises provided by JavaScript?

~~Hibernate can't bypass this so how are we supposed to?~~ I was sort of wrong with this, you can specify an interceptor which uses reflection or other hackery to make this happen.  By default, hibernate requires the constructor.

I think this is expected behavior.  With hibernate, you need a no-parameter constructor - similar to above.

It’s the most ergonomic and accurate TypeScript experience for SQL databases. Hibernate does not require a no-parameter constructor. JPA does (unfortunately). Yes, with Hibernate you'll need to use interceptors and stuff, but that's because Java gives no portable way of bypassing the constructor (there are non-portable ways which involve bytecode manipulations). In Javascript it's easy, Object.create and here you are. After all, what ORM does is a form of serialization, and why on earth would deserialization invoke a constructor? Just think about it.

Anyway, I've switched to mikro-orm a while ago, and do not care anymore.

https://docs.jboss.org/hibernate/orm/5.5/userguide/html_single/Hibernate_User_Guide.html#entity-pojo-constructor

> The entity class should have a no-argument constructor. Both Hibernate and JPA require this.

This can be bypassed by creating a separate interceptor and instantiating your objects using weird allocation or otherwise.

Yes, JavaScript can via `Object.create`.  `mikro-orm` does this by default but allows hitting the constructor.

Perhaps we can do the opposite for now.

> Won't this break the paradigms and promises provided by JavaScript?

After doing a bit more research, the answer is yes.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65395454/object-create-and-native-private-fields

Doing this would break private properties & other features.

We won't make this the default, but I'm gonna open a PR soon.

I have a PR up which implements this.

When deserializing from the database it will not call the constructor if you've set the connection option.

In the future, perhaps we can make that the default.  For now, to prevent some pretty severe breakage I think it's best to have it be opt-in.
